title: Beyond the Estimate: Wiener-Informed Decoding for Easier Training of Pixel-Space Flow Models

paper.title: Beyond the Estimate: Wiener-Informed Decoding for Easier Training of Pixel-Space Flow Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Learning velocity fields directly in pixel space is difficult and slow.
We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning,
with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide.
Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding.
These observations motivate W iener- i nformed D ecoding (WiD),
which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction
and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks.
WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder
and return its predicted coefficient corrections,
with these components initialized with data statistics.
All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective.
Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead.
It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment.
WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions.
On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT
with 37.5% fewer training epochs.
Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Pixel-space flow models offer a simpler generative pipeline, but not an easier learning problem. By operating directly in pixel space, they remove the need for a separate, pretrained autoencoder. However, the denoising network must operate on noisy high-dimensional pixels while learning natural image structure, which makes optimization slow and challenging ( Li & He, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Recent work addresses the challenge in two prominent directions. (i) Prediction-space approaches seek more learnable target parameterizations, such as clean-image prediction ( Li & He, 2026 ) and rank-asymmetric velocity prediction ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . (ii) Architectural approaches distribute contextual modeling and dense pixel prediction across specialized components. For example, DeCo ( Ma et al., 2026 ) and PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026 ) pair a contextual backbone with a fine-grained pixel decoder. These advances make pixel generation more tractable by changing the parameterization or computational organization—and motivate a closer look at the pixel denoising task itself. However, high dimensionality does not imply an absence of exploitable structure. Natural images often possess correlations across space and color, whereas the added Gaussian noise is isotropic. The second-order statistics yield a closed-form linear denoiser— the Wiener estimator ( Wiener, 1949 ; Kailath et al., 2000 ) . Although this estimator cannot capture the full complexity of natural images, it helps previous studies ( Wang & Vastola, 2024 ; Lukoianov et al., 2025 ) investigate the learned denoising behavior and locality. Motivated by these observations, we ask a training question: is it possible to ease pixel-space velocity learning by explicitly providing this statistical estimate? Observation: a fixed estimate already makes a substantial difference. We construct a fixed Wiener estimator from statistics to provide an analytic velocity base and train the DiT ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) to predict the residual correction under the velocity objective. We consider two typical constructions: global DCT ( Ahmed et al., 1974 ) for image-wide spectral structure and patch PCA ( Zhang et al., 2010 ) for local spatial feature. Both analytic bases rescue the otherwise struggling plain DiT (Figure 1(a) ), bringing generation quality into the range of contemporary approaches (Figure 1(b) ). Consequently, even coarse statistical knowledge can ease the burden of velocity learning. (a) Analytic bases rescue direct velocity prediction DiT in pixel space. (b) Analytic bases yield competitive quality under native recipes. (c) WiD provides stronger and more persistent gains on PixelDiT. Figure 1: Analytic Wiener bases ease pixel-space velocity learning. We train B-size models for 40 epochs on ImageNet 256 × 256 256{\times}256 w/o REPA and report FID-10K results w/o CFG. (a) With the same DiT-B/16 setup, adding a DCT or PCA Wiener base rescues the velocity prediction baseline. (b) DiTs with analytic bases reach the performance range of several pixel-space methods. Each method uses its native training and evaluation recipe. (c) When added to native PixelDiT, our Wiener-informed Decoding provides stronger and more sustainable gains than frozen Wiener bases. A frozen statistical prediction is not the whole story. For DiT, our diagnostics further show that much of the reduction in velocity prediction error lies beyond the fitted linear component (Figure 2(a) ). Thus, the effect of Wiener bases is not confined to correcting a linear prediction. This leads us to consider the computation behind the estimate: the Wiener estimator transforms a noisy observation into statistical coordinates, adjusts its coefficients according to the noise level, and maps them back to pixels. Can we go a step further and use these operations to organize the denoiser’s computation, rather than only adding the resulting estimate to its output? Pixel decoding provides a natural and task-aligned interface for this integration. In PixelDiT and DeCo, the backbone provides semantic context, while the decoder maps noisy pixels to velocity— the same input–output task addressed by the Wiener estimator. We observe similar but complementary gains from frozen Wiener bases and pixel decoding (Figure 2(b) ). Our input-perturbation tests support the task alignment: the direct pixel pathway shows closer Wiener alignment than the semantic pathway (Figure 2(c) ). Therefore, we incorporate the estimator’s analysis and synthesis operations into the pixel decoder as trainable components, while retaining the semantic backbone architecture. Approach: from frozen bases to adaptive decoding. We introduce Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD) that incorporates statistical knowledge in two ways. (i) A statistical starting point. Using patch PCA statistics, we initialize a direct prediction path to produce the Wiener velocity estimate. It turns noisy patches into statistical coordinates, scales their coefficients according to the noise level, and maps them back to pixels. (ii) Coordinates for decoder computation. We also allow noisy-patch coordinates to integrate with the decoder’s native input embeddings as additional features. Alongside its original pixel-space velocity output, the decoder also predicts a correction to the coefficient-space estimate. The sum of the Wiener-branch and pixel-head predictions is supervised by the original training objective, and introduced parameters are trained jointly with the network. WiD improves training stability and efficiency, and accommodates different pixel-decoder architectures with a modest parameter increase. Empirically, it reaches comparable generation quality in fewer training steps, with gains that persist further into training than frozen bases (Figure 1(c) ). We validate WiD on class-conditional and text-to-image generation tasks across different resolutions. Contribution Summary. We summarize our contributions as follows. • Observation. We show that coarse statistical estimates can ease pixel-space velocity learning, with error reductions beyond the fitted linear responses. The observation motivates us to use the computation behind the estimate, rather than only its output. • Method. We introduce Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which integrates a trainable statistical prediction path with coefficient-based feature processing and output correction. • Results. We demonstrate improved training stability, efficiency and generation-quality gains across different pixel-decoder architectures with modest overhead.

sections.heading: 2.2 Pixel Decoder Interfaces
sections.text: Architectures such as PixelDiT and DeCo separate contextual modeling from dense pixel prediction. Given a conditioning input y y , their common interface can be written as s = ℬ ⁡ ( z t , t , y ) , v ^ = 𝒟 ⁡ ( z t , s ) , s=\mathcal{B}(z_{t},t,y),\qquad\hat{v}=\mathcal{D}(z_{t},s), (6) where ℬ \mathcal{B} is a contextual backbone, s s denotes the conditioning features, and 𝒟 \mathcal{D} is the pixel decoder. Although the internal blocks may differ, the interface remains consistent. The decoder embeds noisy pixels, processes features under contextual modulation, and maps the features to a velocity prediction. We explain how to incorporate Wiener-informed operations into this interface in Section 4 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Beyond the Additive Linear Prediction
sections.text: An analytic base supplies a prediction that the network would otherwise have to learn. But does it also help the network learn the remaining prediction? We investigate this by comparing the velocity predictions with a well-trained reference model: the official PixelDiT-XL checkpoint at 320 epoch. At each fixed t t , we fit an affine prediction ℓ f \ell_{f} from z t z_{t} to each model’s complete velocity output f f , and similarly fit ℓ ref \ell_{\rm ref} to the reference f ref f_{\rm ref} . For PCA, the fit is a shared patch-affine map; for DCT, it includes independent RGB-affine maps at each frequency. Each affine family contains the corresponding frozen Wiener base as a zero-bias special case, and subtracting the fitted response removes its explicit additive contribution. (9) We fit by least squares on 4,096 4{,}096 validation images and score on 3,072 3{,}072 disjoint images with two fixed noise draws each. Figure 2(a) reports the reduction in each error while applying Wiener bases to DiT, averaged over five time points. We observe that the remaining prediction contributes most of the improvement, and that the linear-error reduction shrinks with training. These results suggest that a frozen base does more than provide a better starting prediction: it may also help the network organize its computation to learn the remaining prediction more effectively.

We examine its effect using the same reference and patch-affine decomposition as above. To pursue more persistent gains, we make the estimator’s prediction path and coordinate transforms trainable parts of the decoder, allowing them to evolve with learning (Section 4 ).

sections.heading: 4 Wiener-informed Decoding

sections.heading: 5.1 Class-to-Image Generation
sections.text: Setup. We choose PixelDiT-XL/16 ( Yu et al., 2026 ) as the backbone to evaluate our Wiener-informed Decoding on class-conditional ImageNet ( Deng et al., 2009 ) generation. Following its original training recipe, we use AdamW optimizer ( Kingma & Ba, 2015 ; Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019 ) with the learning rate of 1e-4 for the first 160 epochs, and then step down to 1e-5 on ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 . For ImageNet 512 × 512 512\times 512 , we fine-tune the 260-epoch 256 × 256 256\times 256 checkpoint for 50 epochs. The global batch size of 256 and REPA using DINOv2-B ( Oquab et al., 2024 ) with weight 0.5 remain the same. As is stated in Section 3.1 , we use 51,200 images (about 4% of the training set) to compute the spatial patch statistics to initialize WiD. The computation costs us only 1 minute with one GPU and 12 CPU DataLoader workers, which we consider quite practical in large-scale training scenarios. sections.heading: 6.1 Statistical Denoising
sections.text: Statistical priors for image restoration. Wiener estimation has a long history in image denoising and restoration ( Wiener, 1949 ) . Methods such as BLS-GSM ( Portilla et al., 2003 ) and NL-Bayes ( Lebrun et al., 2013 ) build on Wiener estimation using statistics for image denoising. Similar to statistical operations in our WiD, BM3D ( Dabov et al., 2007 ) organizes computation by constructing representations, applying empirical Wiener filtering to coefficients, and reconstructing the image through inverse transforms. Furthermore, Deep Wiener Deconvolution ( Dong et al., 2020 ) has proposed to integrate Wiener operations into a learnable feature-processing pipeline for image deblurring. Together, these studies show how statistical priors can be constructed and utilized. Statistical structure in diffusion. In studies of diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , statistical estimates also provide a way to understand learned denoisers. Linear fits reveal Gaussian structure associated with generalization ( Li et al., 2024 ) , while Gaussian score approximations capture moderate and high noise-level behavior and help accelerate sampling ( Wang & Vastola, 2024 ) . Data statistics can also explain locality patterns otherwise attributed to architecture ( Lukoianov et al., 2025 ) . These findings connect classical estimation to modern generative models, and inspire us to explore using statistical priors in generative learning. From estimation to generative learning. Motivated by these insights, our research takes a step further to study how this statistical knowledge can aid pixel-space velocity learning: WiD uses the statistics to initialize the prediction path as a structured starting point, and integrates the computational operations and coordinates into the decoder.

sections.heading: 6.2 Pixel-space Flow Models
sections.text: Prediction parameterization. Recent approaches ease pixel-space learning by changing what the network predicts. JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) predicts clean images, while AsymFlow ( Chen et al., 2026a ) combines full-rank data prediction with low-rank noise prediction to reconstruct the velocity. Recently, k k -Diff ( Jin & Wang, 2026 ) learns a scalar that controls the data–noise mixture predicted by the network, while retaining velocity-space supervision. A simplified linear analysis motivates this parameterization by relating the preferred mixture to data dimensionality. Separately, WiD aims to address the similar learning difficulty within velocity prediction. Pixel decoding. Another direction is to separate contextual modeling from dense pixel prediction. PixNerd ( Wang et al., 2026a ) uses patch-wise neural fields, PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026 ) uses pixel transformers, and DeCo ( Ma et al., 2026 ) uses context-conditioned MLP decoders to alleviate the learning difficulty. WiD builds on this separation: it retains the native backbone and decoder blocks in PixelDiT and DeCo, adding statistical interfaces around their existing computation. Connection to preconditioning. Preconditioning addresses differences in scale and geometry that can hinder diffusion and flow training. EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) normalizes network inputs and residual targets using noise-dependent scaling and a skip connection. Preconditioned Flow Matching ( Ahamed et al., 2026 ) instead uses reversible data transformations to improve the conditioning of intermediate flow distributions. WiD is related in the use of statistical structure to ease learning, but focuses on decoder design: a trainable Wiener prediction path interacts with the native decoder.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We present Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD) to improve the velocity learning of pixel-space flow models. Specifically, we have shown that coarse second-order statistics can ease pixel-space training, and the gains from frozen Wiener bases extend beyond their explicit linear predictions. Motivated by these insights, we developed WiD, which combines a trainable statistical prediction path with coefficient interfaces that connect it to the native pixel decoder. We demonstrate that WiD enhances training efficiency and stability while consistently improving generation quality across model scales and decoder architectures, benefiting both class-conditional and text-to-image generation with modest parameter overhead. These findings suggest that statistical denoisers can contribute beyond the estimate: the computational organization is also helpful for learning pixel-space generation.

sections.heading: Appendix C Limitations and Future Work
sections.text: In this work, we mainly focus on easing velocity learning for pixel-space image generation tasks. Actually, we think the perspective of statistical denoising may also be helpful for other flow generative models. Therefore, explorations of integrating statistical denoisers into other generative tasks are also attractive directions, such as latent space generation, and language, audio, as well as video generation. In the future, we are planning to improve upon our current approach, and take a step further to explore the potential of integrating Wiener-informed structures directly into diffusion transformers, and try to develop next foundation architecture for flow-matching tasks.

We show that coarse second-order image statistics can ease this task: frozen Wiener estimates improve velocity learning, with gains extending beyond the linear predictions they explicitly provide. Moreover, we observe similar but complementary gains from frozen bases and pixel decoding. These observations motivate W iener- i nformed D ecoding (WiD), which uses statistical knowledge both for direct prediction and to organize decoder computation without modifying native blocks. WiD combines a trainable Wiener prediction path with coefficient interfaces that inject features into the native decoder and return its predicted coefficient corrections, with these components initialized with data statistics. All introduced parameters, including the spectrum and coordinate transforms, are trained jointly under the original pixel-space velocity objective. Across model scales and decoder architectures, WiD accelerates training and improves generation quality with modest parameter overhead. It also yields smoother gradient trajectories and remains effective with representation alignment. WiD improves class-conditional and text-to-image generation across different resolutions. On ImageNet 256 × 256 256\times 256 , PixelDiT-XL with WiD reaches FID 1.53 after 500 epochs, achieving comparable quality to PixelDiT with 37.5% fewer training epochs. Statistical denoisers contribute beyond the estimate: their computational structure can also ease pixel-space training. 1 Introduction Pixel-space flow models offer a simpler generative pipeline, but not an easier learning problem. By operating directly in pixel space, they remove the need for a separate, pretrained autoencoder. However, the denoising network must operate on noisy high-dimensional pixels while learning natural image structure, which makes optimization slow and challenging ( Li & He, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Recent work addresses the challenge in two prominent directions. (i) Prediction-space approaches seek more learnable target parameterizations, such as clean-image prediction ( Li & He, 2026 ) and rank-asymmetric velocity prediction ( Chen et al., 2026a ) . (ii) Architectural approaches distribute contextual modeling and dense pixel prediction across specialized components. For example, DeCo ( Ma et al., 2026 ) and PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026 ) pair a contextual backbone with a fine-grained pixel decoder. These advances make pixel generation more tractable by changing the parameterization or computational organization—and motivate a closer look at the pixel denoising task itself. However, high dimensionality does not imply an absence of exploitable structure. Natural images often possess correlations across space and color, whereas the added Gaussian noise is isotropic. The second-order statistics yield a closed-form linear denoiser— the Wiener estimator ( Wiener, 1949 ; Kailath et al., 2000 ) . Although this estimator cannot capture the full complexity of natural images, it helps previous studies ( Wang & Vastola, 2024 ; Lukoianov et al., 2025 ) investigate the learned denoising behavior and locality. Motivated by these observations, we ask a training question: is it possible to ease pixel-space velocity learning by explicitly providing this statistical estimate? Observation: a fixed estimate already makes a substantial difference. We construct a fixed Wiener estimator from statistics to provide an analytic velocity base and train the DiT ( Peebles & Xie, 2023 ) to predict the residual correction under the velocity objective. We consider two typical constructions: global DCT ( Ahmed et al., 1974 ) for image-wide spectral structure and patch PCA ( Zhang et al., 2010 ) for local spatial feature. Both analytic bases rescue the otherwise struggling plain DiT (Figure 1(a) ), bringing generation quality into the range of contemporary approaches (Figure 1(b) ). Consequently, even coarse statistical knowledge can ease the burden of velocity learning. (a) Analytic bases rescue direct velocity prediction DiT in pixel space. (b) Analytic bases yield competitive quality under native recipes. (c) WiD provides stronger and more persistent gains on PixelDiT. Figure 1: Analytic Wiener bases ease pixel-space velocity learning. We train B-size models for 40 epochs on ImageNet 256 × 256 256{\times}256 w/o REPA and report FID-10K results w/o CFG. (a) With the same DiT-B/16 setup, adding a DCT or PCA Wiener base rescues the velocity prediction baseline. (b) DiTs with analytic bases reach the performance range of several pixel-space methods. Each method uses its native training and evaluation recipe. (c) When added to native PixelDiT, our Wiener-informed Decoding provides stronger and more sustainable gains than frozen Wiener bases. A frozen statistical prediction is not the whole story. For DiT, our diagnostics further show that much of the reduction in velocity prediction error lies beyond the fitted linear component (Figure 2(a) ). Thus, the effect of Wiener bases is not confined to correcting a linear prediction. This leads us to consider the computation behind the estimate: the Wiener estimator transforms a noisy observation into statistical coordinates, adjusts its coefficients according to the noise level, and maps them back to pixels. Can we go a step further and use these operations to organize the denoiser’s computation, rather than only adding the resulting estimate to its output? Pixel decoding provides a natural and task-aligned interface for this integration. In PixelDiT and DeCo, the backbone provides semantic context, while the decoder maps noisy pixels to velocity— the same input–output task addressed by the Wiener estimator. We observe similar but complementary gains from frozen Wiener bases and pixel decoding (Figure 2(b) ). Our input-perturbation tests support the task alignment: the direct pixel pathway shows closer Wiener alignment than the semantic pathway (Figure 2(c) ). Therefore, we incorporate the estimator’s analysis and synthesis operations into the pixel decoder as trainable components, while retaining the semantic backbone architecture. Approach: from frozen bases to adaptive decoding. We introduce Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD) that incorporates statistical knowledge in two ways. (i) A statistical starting point. Using patch PCA statistics, we initialize a direct prediction path to produce the Wiener velocity estimate. It turns noisy patches into statistical coordinates, scales their coefficients according to the noise level, and maps them back to pixels. (ii) Coordinates for decoder computation. We also allow noisy-patch coordinates to integrate with the decoder’s native input embeddings as additional features. Alongside its original pixel-space velocity output, the decoder also predicts a correction to the coefficient-space estimate. The sum of the Wiener-branch and pixel-head predictions is supervised by the original training objective, and introduced parameters are trained jointly with the network. WiD improves training stability and efficiency, and accommodates different pixel-decoder architectures with a modest parameter increase. Empirically, it reaches comparable generation quality in fewer training steps, with gains that persist further into training than frozen bases (Figure 1(c) ). We validate WiD on class-conditional and text-to-image generation tasks across different resolutions. Contribution Summary. We summarize our contributions as follows. • Observation. We show that coarse statistical estimates can ease pixel-space velocity learning, with error reductions beyond the fitted linear responses. The observation motivates us to use the computation behind the estimate, rather than only its output. • Method. We introduce Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD), which integrates a trainable statistical prediction path with coefficient-based feature processing and output correction. • Results. Wiener estimation has a long history in image denoising and restoration ( Wiener, 1949 ) . Methods such as BLS-GSM ( Portilla et al., 2003 ) and NL-Bayes ( Lebrun et al., 2013 ) build on Wiener estimation using statistics for image denoising. Similar to statistical operations in our WiD, BM3D ( Dabov et al., 2007 ) organizes computation by constructing representations, applying empirical Wiener filtering to coefficients, and reconstructing the image through inverse transforms. Furthermore, Deep Wiener Deconvolution ( Dong et al., 2020 ) has proposed to integrate Wiener operations into a learnable feature-processing pipeline for image deblurring. Together, these studies show how statistical priors can be constructed and utilized. Statistical structure in diffusion. In studies of diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) , statistical estimates also provide a way to understand learned denoisers. Linear fits reveal Gaussian structure associated with generalization ( Li et al., 2024 ) , while Gaussian score approximations capture moderate and high noise-level behavior and help accelerate sampling ( Wang & Vastola, 2024 ) . Data statistics can also explain locality patterns otherwise attributed to architecture ( Lukoianov et al., 2025 ) . These findings connect classical estimation to modern generative models, and inspire us to explore using statistical priors in generative learning. From estimation to generative learning. Motivated by these insights, our research takes a step further to study how this statistical knowledge can aid pixel-space velocity learning: WiD uses the statistics to initialize the prediction path as a structured starting point, and integrates the computational operations and coordinates into the decoder. 6.2 Pixel-space Flow Models Prediction parameterization. Recent approaches ease pixel-space learning by changing what the network predicts. JiT ( Li & He, 2026 ) predicts clean images, while AsymFlow ( Chen et al., 2026a ) combines full-rank data prediction with low-rank noise prediction to reconstruct the velocity. Recently, k k -Diff ( Jin & Wang, 2026 ) learns a scalar that controls the data–noise mixture predicted by the network, while retaining velocity-space supervision. A simplified linear analysis motivates this parameterization by relating the preferred mixture to data dimensionality. Separately, WiD aims to address the similar learning difficulty within velocity prediction. Pixel decoding. Another direction is to separate contextual modeling from dense pixel prediction. PixNerd ( Wang et al., 2026a ) uses patch-wise neural fields, PixelDiT ( Yu et al., 2026 ) uses pixel transformers, and DeCo ( Ma et al., 2026 ) uses context-conditioned MLP decoders to alleviate the learning difficulty. WiD builds on this separation: it retains the native backbone and decoder blocks in PixelDiT and DeCo, adding statistical interfaces around their existing computation. Connection to preconditioning. Preconditioning addresses differences in scale and geometry that can hinder diffusion and flow training. EDM ( Karras et al., 2022 ) normalizes network inputs and residual targets using noise-dependent scaling and a skip connection. Preconditioned Flow Matching ( Ahamed et al., 2026 ) instead uses reversible data transformations to improve the conditioning of intermediate flow distributions. WiD is related in the use of statistical structure to ease learning, but focuses on decoder design: a trainable Wiener prediction path interacts with the native decoder. 7 Conclusion We present Wiener-informed Decoding (WiD) to improve the velocity learning of pixel-space flow models. Specifically, we have shown that coarse second-order statistics can ease pixel-space training, and the gains from frozen Wiener bases extend beyond their explicit linear predictions.
